title: The Double Life of Véronique is a beautiful and deeply layered film that challenges you on a philosophical level

commenti.body: Damn, I just watched this film for the first time! What a coincidence seeing this post. Anyway, I've felt deeply moved by the film but I don't know why. First I thought was the use of colour, then I thought it was the mistery or the characters, but it might be all of it. I'll read your post carefully tomorrow, OP, but maybe I need to see this film again.

You raise some interesting questions toward the end of your post, particularly when it comes to Véronique's relationship with Alexandre and the significance of puppetry in the film. I wonder whether you would agree with the statement that Véronique displays an inability to self-actualize (as opposed to Weronika) and is thus a tragic character. 

Since you brought up Preisner and "Van den Budenmayer," perhaps you would be interested in further analysis of "Van den Budenmayer: Concerto en Mi Mineur," along with other images that appear in the film, that support such a statement. 

To start, did you know that the lyrics to the song (which are not subtitled in the film), come from Canto II, *Paradiso*, by Dante? The lyrics read:  
  
**O Ye, who in some pretty little boat,**  
  
**Eager to listen, have been following**  
  
**Behind my ship, that singing sails along,**  
  
**Turn back to look again upon your shores;**  
  
**Do not put out to sea, lest peradventure,**  
  
**In losing me, you might yourselves be lost.**  
  
**The sea I sail has never yet been passed;**  
  
**Minerva breathes, and pilots me Apollo,**  
  
**And Muses nine point out to me the Bears.**  
  
Some context: these lines, with the rest of early cantos, tell us of the first of Nine Spheres of Heaven--originally conceived of as stars--which are above Earth. This is inverse to the Circles of the Inferno; the sequence of the Spheres serve a similar function, in that they represent virtues (rather than vices), and are stages to Heaven. It's fitting then, that the film's opening scene features the main character as a child gazing up at the stars.  
  
According to Dante, the Moon is the first Sphere; it symbolizes inconstancy, doubt, and infortitude, due to its waxing and waning phases. This can be seen of course in the motif of doubles (or halves) in the film, which take several forms. The closest visual is that of the orb through which Véronique looks and daydreams of alternate life paths.  
  
In *Paradiso*, breaking one's vows (or being inconstant to one's chosen path) would limit oneself to the first Sphere and unable to attain the higher stages. Hence the warning contained in the opening lines of the canto, which Weronika sings: those unready to ascend, should refrain from going further, otherwise they will be fated to a lesser paradise. Weronika literally dies and it could be argued that the successive use of POV shots in Weronika's final scene depict her soul's depature from the body, not just Véronique's perspective. If this is the case, then we should note that though her soul ascends, it does not travel far, much like the souls in *Paradiso*.  
  
This causes Véronique to abandon that potential path. But she seems lost, unable to decide or be satisfied with one path, as she is afflicted to dream and wonder. **(Here your observations on Alexandre and his role as a puppeteer to Véronique's puppet seem relevant. Perhaps I misread the film but the final scene with Alexandre and Véronique seems unsettling and even sinister.)** The film's closing scene could be read as depicting Véronique stuck in the Sphere of Inconstancy, a permanent state of latency due to this affliction; she touches the tree, both of them much larger than when she was a child and could hold a leaf in her hands and wonder about all of life's possibilities, as she realizes how real and lifelike her existence has become. She wonders again, what the tree might have been, imagining it cut down and as lumber in her father's workshop. Her tendency to dream about double lives is something she cannot help but continue, which is also why she will never be satisfied or feel whole.  
  
Whether the inconstancy of her own life, is a universal reflection on the human condition or the individual cause of her anxiety as well as what is to do about it, is a matter of further interpretation: should she commit to a path of finitude or be forever lost to the mysteries of her own existence? If these are questions that are posed in the film, I don't believe they are fully answered; though I do think Kieślowski elaborates on these questions in his next work (the *Three Colours* trilogy).
Wow, thats very interesting about the lyrics! Everything you said is an interesting perspective to look at the film. And yes, I would agree that Véronique could be looked at as a tragic character

>I've felt deeply moved by the film but I don't know why.

This is exactly what I had too and why I rewatched it. There is something really interesting about this film, something that isn't particularly clear to me

This is one of my favorites and it goes beyond analysis for me. Kieslowski is like a magician. He asks questions that he doesn't know the answer to. Everything about that movie is so intoxicating - the imagery, the score, Irene Jacob, that feeling of impending doom. It's a mysterious film.

The Double Life of Veronique was the first art/foreign film I chose to go to, at age 19 or 20. I didn't know anything about it but it was playing at the art museum instead of a movie theater; my city growing up didn't have a theater that showed that kind of movie. 

How it had such an emotional effect on me was a mystery, a magic trick of cinema. The story was completely outside my expectations and understanding of how the world works. What actually happened? How? What does it mean? What does "the meaning of a movie" even mean? 

I couldn't explain it afterward. But the end of the movie was overwhelming.

That kind of experience was addictive.
This is the exact same feeling I had. I couldn't really place it why I loved it so much. The only thing I was sure of, was THAT I loved it
